chain.g: (intransitive) to labor, strive, exert oneself, suffer, be in distress, (transitive) to work out, elaborate

ety.text: From Middle English labouren, from Old French laborer, from Latin laborare (“(intransitive) to labor, strive, exert oneself, suffer, be in distress, (transitive) to work out, elaborate”), from labor (“labor, toil, work, exertion”); perhaps remotely akin to robur (“strength”). Displaced native English swink (“toil, labor”).

senses.d: An effort expended on a particular task; toil, work.
That which requires hard work for its accomplishment; that which demands effort.
ex: Being a labour of so great difficulty, the exact performance thereof we may rather wish than look for.

senses.d: Workers in general; the working class, the workforce; sometimes specifically the labour movement, organised labour.
A political party or force aiming or claiming to represent the interests of labour.
The act or process of a mother giving birth.
ex: Near-synonyms: childbirth, parturition
Paul Doherty came to the rescue when his wife Georgina went into labour early just minutes from their local hospital.

senses.d: The time period during which a mother gives birth.

senses.d: A group of moles.

ex: "Crab" 2-6-0 No 42802 labours up to Beattock Summit with a northbound freight from Carlisle in August 1960.

senses.d: To belabour, to emphasise or expand upon (a point in a debate, etc).
ex: I think we've all got the idea. There's no need to labour the point.

senses.d: To be oppressed with difficulties or disease; to do one's work under conditions which make it especially hard or wearisome; to move slowly, as against opposition, or under a burden.
ex: the stone that labours up the hill
The line too labours, and the words move slow.

senses.d: To suffer the pangs of childbirth.
To pitch or roll heavily, as a ship in a turbulent sea.
ex: the ship laboured so much, and took in so much water in her upper works, that we could neither eat, nor sleep dry

ety.text: From Middle English label (“narrow band, strip of cloth”), from Old French label, lambel (Modern French lambeau), from Frankish *lappā (“torn piece of cloth”), from Proto-Germanic *lappǭ, *lappô (“cloth stuff, rag, scraps, flap, dewlap, lobe, rabbit ear”), from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“blade”). Cognate with Old High German lappa (“rag, piece of cloth”), Old English læppa (“skirt, flap of a garment”). More at lap.

senses.d: A small ticket or sign giving information about something to which it is attached or intended to be attached.
ex: We laughed at her because the label was still on her new sweater.
The label says this silk scarf should not be washed in the washing machine.

senses.d: A name given to something or someone to categorise them as part of a particular social group.
ex: Ever since he started going to the rock club, he's been given the label "waster".

senses.d: A company that sells records.
ex: The label signed the band after hearing a demo tape.

senses.d: A user-defined alias for a numerical designation, the reverse of an enumeration.
ex: Storage devices can be given by label or ID.
